Grade 6 - World Geography and Ancient Civilization II - Latin America, South
and East Asia, Oceania, Latin America, and Europe (Draft)
Overview

In grade 6, students will examine how movement and migration impacted the interactions between expanding civilizations through conquest and trade, including the physical and political geography and ancient societies of South and East Asia, Oceania, Latin America, and Europe. Students will note how geography, power, wealth, and religion influence culture, change, and development within civilizations as they examine how the perspectives of political science, economics, geography, history, and archaeology apply to the study of regions and countries. Students will develop an appreciation of cultural contributions (art, music, literature, architecture) and lasting achievements in science and technology. Grade 6 concludes with a study of government in Greece and Rome, which serves as a prelude to the study of civics in grade 8. Through an understanding of ancient history, students will develop an appreciation for the foundations of the modern world.
Looking Back

In grade 5, students examined how movement and migration impacted the interactions between expanding civilizations through conquest and trade, including the emergence and development of early societies in Western Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa.
Looking Ahead

In grade 7, students will build on their knowledge of Vermont and United States politics, geography, economics, and history as they re-visit the conflicts over slavery that continued into Reconstruction and beyond and led to the long struggle in the 19th and 20th centuries for civil rights.

Inquiry

Why inquiry? Using inquiry as an instructional model for the teaching of social studies allows students to authentically ask questions, search for and analyze evidence, and provide explanations and arguments to challenges facing their world.

The inquiry instructional model is driven by authentic questions or problems that have relevance for children. Students learn content, skills, and dispositions as they seek answers to questions and as they apply their learning to take informed action. Pioneered by Dewey (1938), inquiry is an attempt to make classroom experiences feel more like the authentic, curiosity-driven experiences that motivate learning outside of school. (Using Inquiry to Prepare Students for College, Career, and Civic Life, elementary edition, p. 22)

The Inquiry Arc is defined in Dimension 1 (questioning) of the College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework for Social Studies State Standards. In this Framework, Dimension 3 (evidence sourcing), and Dimension 4 (communicating), as well as some evidence indicators found within Dimension 2 – History, have been combined with Dimension 1 into a singular Inquiry Process, as evidenced below. This Inquiry Process begins in the elementary grades and increases in depth and complexity as it spans through high school, preparing students to spiral their learning and skill acquisition in the social studies for college and career readiness.
Inquiry Process (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.

Civilizations • Maya – Law/rules codified in hieroglyphs, enforced by kings; Religious and social order through kings and priests; city-state specific; severe punishments, order maintained; theocratic-monarchy; elite councils • Inca – Centralized under Sapa Inca; no written laws but quipu records; unity, labor, infrastructure; strict top-down governance; mit'a labor system; social stability, but little personal freedom; autocratic; centralized bureaucracy; resource control; religious/social order. • Aztec – Codified laws; many in Codex Mendoza; war, tribute, religious order; military and religious enforcers; centralized from Tenochtitlán; harsh penalties; strict social hierarchy; emperor advised by noble councils; codification of crimes, imperial authority. • Ancient China – Legalism, Confucianism; written codes (e.g., Qin and Han laws); harmony, obedience, order; imperial bureaucracy, scholar-officials; dynastic cycle; public works, exams; centralized monarchy; civil service; meritocratic/bureaucratic governance. • Ancient India – Dharma and Manusmriti; caste-based laws; social hierarchy, religious duty; local assemblies and royal courts; rigid caste system, but order preserved; mixed: monarchies, republics, village panchayats; religious diversity, moral principles. • Oceania – Oral laws; kapu system (sacred prohibitions); maintain divine order, resource control; chiefs enforced spiritual taboos; social cohesion but limited mobility; chiefdoms; consensus in councils; adherence to tradition, cultural practices. • Ancient Greece – Written laws; e.g., Draco, Solon; justice, equality (esp. in Athens); citizen assemblies, courts; flourishing of democracy, but instability; varied: democracy (Athens), oligarchy (Sparta); democratic laws, civic participation.

Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections

Students will be able to explain how markets in early civilizations facilitated the exchange of goods, services, and labor. Students will be able to explain human, natural, and capital resources in early civilizations.

• Barter and exchange, Commodity money, precious metals, transition to metal coins • Economic specialization, labor systems – slave labor, caste systems, bureaucracies, craftsmen, artisans, trade guilds; natural resources – agriculture, mining, fishing, timber; trade networks. Maya – Primarily barter system; cacao beans and obsidian used as a form of currency. Inca – No formal money system; used quipu (knotted strings) for record-keeping; relied heavily on mit’a labor tax and barter. Aztec – Barter-based; cacao beans and cotton cloth (called quachtli) used as currency. Ancient China – Early use of cowry shells; later, bronze coins; during the Zhou and Qin dynasties, round coins with square holes became common. Ancient India – Barter system early on; later, silver and copper coins were introduced by the Maurya and Gupta Empires. Oceania – Mostly barter; some used shell money (e.g., in Solomon Islands); trade occurred between islands for resources. Ancient Greece – Used coins (silver, bronze); Athens’ currency was the drachma; trade was significant in city-states.

Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections
Students will explain how the costs and benefits of trade between early civilizations contributed to cultural development, economic growth, and interdependence.

Cross-cutting: Cultural exchange – colonization conquests, trade, spread of religion; economic impact – trade; political changes – development of city-states, rise and fall of empires • Geographic barriers – mountainous terrain, islands, lakes, varied/vast landscapes, deserts • Lack of technology/transportation – limited advancements • Infrastructure – not well-developed • Internal strife, external invasions, military campaigns disrupt • Political barriers – wars, closed borders • Cultural/language differences Incas (South America – Andes Mountains) • Barriers: Steep mountains, lack of wheeled vehicles, no written language. • Impact: Trade was mostly local. Used llama caravans and built roads and bridges to connect their empire.

Aztecs (Central Mexico) • Barriers: Swampy land (Lake Texcoco), surrounded by rivals. • Impact: Built chinampas (floating gardens) to create fertile farmland on swampy lakebeds; Constructed causeways, dikes, and canals to connect their island capital and control flooding; Developed strong military alliances (Triple Alliance) to defend against and dominate neighboring rivals. Mayas (Mesoamerica – jungles) • Barriers: Dense rainforests, lack of rivers for easy transport. • Impact: Trade was by foot or canoe, often limited in distance. Cities traded luxury goods like jade and cacao. Ancient China • Barriers: Deserts (Gobi), mountains (Himalayas), oceans. • Impact: Limited early contact with the West but eventually created the Silk Road to trade goods like silk and porcelain. Ancient India • Barriers: Himalayas, monsoon seasons. • Impact: Mountains blocked northern trade, but rivers and seas enabled trade with Mesopotamia and East Africa. Major center for spice and textile trade. Ancient Greece • Barriers: Mountains divided city-states, poor farmland. • Impact: Encouraged sea trade and colonization. Greeks became skilled sailors trading olive oil, wine, pottery.

Ancient Rome • Barriers: Few natural barriers within empire, but external threats and pirates. • Impact: Created roads and protected sea routes. Controlled trade across Europe, Asia, and Africa Ancient Oceania (Pacific Islands) • Barriers: Vast ocean distances, limited natural resources. • Impact: Used canoes and star navigation to trade items like obsidian, shells, and food. Trade was inter-island and risky. War and conflict can: • Damage trade and reduce wealth • Destroy farmland and cities • Increase taxes or tribute to fund armies • Shift power between regions or leaders • Sometimes lead to new resources through conquest Incas: • Conflict Impact: Civil war weakened the empire just before Spanish arrival. • Economic Effects: War disrupted farming and the mita labor system, damaging food production and infrastructure; after conquest, Spanish took gold/silver.

Aztecs: • Conflict Impact: Constant warfare to collect tribute and captives. Economic Effects: Empire grew rich from tribute, but the system was unstable—many enemies joined the Spanish to overthrow the Aztecs, ending their economy. Mayas: • Conflict Impact: Frequent city-state wars. • Economic Effects: Wars weakened agriculture, led to abandoned cities, and disrupted long-distance trade. Likely contributed to the collapse of some major cities. Ancient China: • Conflict Impact: Long periods of war, like the Warring States Period. • Economic Effects: War destroyed farmland and displaced people, but also pushed innovation in infrastructure (roads, canals, walls). Unified under empires like the Han helped restore trade. Ancient India: • Conflict Impact: Invasions (e.g., by Persians, Greeks, Huns). • Economic Effects: Some wars hurt trade routes like the Silk Road; others, like the Maurya Empire's unification, boosted trade and taxes. War created shifts in power and economic stability.

Ancient Greece: • Conflict Impact: Wars between city-states (l Peloponnesian War) and with outsiders (like Persians). Economic Effects: Wars drained resources, destroyed crops, and disrupted trade. Athens, once rich, lost power and wealth after the Peloponnesian War. Ancient Rome: • Conflict Impact: Frequent wars of conquest and later civil wars. • Economic Effects: Early conquests brought wealth and slaves, growing the economy. But later wars drained resources, ruined trade, and contributed to Rome's decline. Oceania: • Conflict Impact: Small-scale tribal wars and resource competition. • Economic Effects: Limited warfare due to isolation, but conflicts could damage canoes, crops, or cause population loss, reducing trade and food security.

Ancient Math and Music - PBS Learning Media: Explore how Pythagoras and Plato found mathematics in music and nature in this video from NOVA: The Great Math Mystery. The ancient Greeks identified three pleasing musical intervals: an octave, a fifth, and a fourth. Pythagoras discovered that the beautiful musical relationship between the notes was also a mathematical relationship: the harmonious sounds are produced by vibrating strings with particular ratios of string length. Plato believed geometry and mathematics exist in their own ideal world and that certain shapes (now known as the Platonic solids) were associated with the classical elements from which the world was made - earth, fire, air, water, and the universe; discussion questions provided.

Chinese Innovation - C3 IDM: This IDM is described as being for grades 3-5 but can be utilized in Grade 6 with minimal adaptation. This inquiry provides students with an opportunity to examine nine of China’s most impactful innovations and their contributions to the modern world. These innovations and inventions fall into three categories: 1) Communication innovations, including written language, paper, and printing; 2) Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) innovations, including the compass, the Great Wall of China, gunpowder, and fireworks, and; 3) Economic innovations, including common currency, silk, and the Silk Road.

Mapping Populations: The Ancient World - PBS Learning Media: Students will study choropleth maps of the ancient world, and the population density changes from 3000 BC to 1 CE. Then, they will fill out a chart about the major influential factors in population density, and answer questions about the map.

Nomadic Life - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of prehistoric nomadic life. By investigating the compelling question “How do we know the past without written evidence?” students evaluate how nomads communicated, where they lived, and how they defined their needs based on the places they lived. The formative performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students develop understanding of nomadic life to compare with agrarian life. Students create an evidence-based argument about how non- written artifacts support understanding of nomadic life during prehistoric times.

Where in China Is…? - PBS Learning Media: In this activity, students examine and plot different locations that hold historical importance. Students will also use the interactive game Where in China is...? to study and test their knowledge of Chinese geography.

Writings of the Ancient Maya - PBS Learning Media: In this interactive lesson supporting literacy skills, students are introduced to the ancient Mayan civilization through their writings. Students develop their literacy skills as they explore a social studies focus on the destruction of many Mayan writings by the Spanish and what archaeologists have learned from the writings that remain. During this process, they read informational text, learn and practice vocabulary words, and explore content through a video and interactive activities.

Sample Content Connections

Students will be able to identify and explain multiple causes and effects of key events and developments in early civilizations. Students will be able to explain the environmental impacts of human innovation on early civilizations.

Cross-cutting concepts: Trade and cultural exchange, language, cultural assimilation, colonization conquests, spread of religion; political changes – development of city-states, rise and fall of empires • Government/leadership structure • Culture (e.g., religion/beliefs, accepted practices/traditions) • Specialization of labor • Mastery of food supply • Technology • Economic systems • Education • Communication systems (e.g., spoken language, alphabetic and/or numeric systems, hieroglyphics, illustrations)
Resources

An Age of Empires and Interchange - History Project UC-Irvine: What were the effects of the exchanges on the Silk Road?” and “What is Hellenistic culture and how did it spread among regions in Afroeurasia?” are just two of the 6th grade Curricular Resources provided by the History Project, which allows students to study the characteristics of the ancient civilizations (social, political, religious, economic, and cultural), and how they were able to grow in size, complexity, and power.

Ancient Greece and Rome - Core Knowledge: Free downloadable curriculum; Scroll to bottom of page to download individual PDF documents: Teacher Guide and Student Reader. Guide provides activities, assessments and literary selections.

Angkor What? Angkor Wat! - National Endowment for the Humanities: Beginning in the 9th century, the Khmer empire, which was based in what is today northwestern Cambodia, began to gather power and territory in mainland Southeast Asia. It would grow to be one of the largest empires in Southeast Asian history. In this lesson, students will learn about Angkor Wat and its place in Cambodian, and Southeast Asian, history. Students will attempt to ‘read’ the temple, in a way which resembles the reading of a primary document, to gain insight into this history.

Aztec - C3 IDM: This annotated inquiry is listed as for 9th grade, but the compelling question, “What Do the Buried Secrets of Tenochtitlán Tell Us About the Aztecs?” and the staging question, where students look at photographs of the excavation of Tenochtitlán in 2012, can be used/adapted for 6th graders to formulate questions about the Aztec city.

Feudal Japan - Core Knowledge: Scroll to bottom of page to download individual PDF documents: Teacher Guide (p. 77-153) and Student Reader. Guide provides activities, assessments and literary selections; focused on grade 5.

Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, and Zheng He-Early Connectors - PBS Learning Media: In this lesson, students will explore the adventures of these three world travelers. After viewing three short videos about their journeys, students will analyze photographs of a city that all three travelers visited, write a log entry describing a sighting of Zheng He’s fleet of ships, and then read excerpts from Marco Polo’s and Ibn Battuta’s accounts of their journeys. The lesson will conclude with students writing a short play in which the three travelers meet and share stories of their adventures.

Maya, Aztec, and Inca Civilizations - Core Knowledge: Free downloadable curriculum; Scroll to bottom of page to download individual PDF documents: Teacher Guide and Student Reader. Guide provides activities, assessments and literary selections; grade 5 level.

Native America - PBS Learning Media: This Native America collection reaches back 15,000 years, examining ancient city planning and early systems of science and spirituality and extends to present-day exploration of Indigenous knowledge and language preservation; focus on Incas and Aztecs with video clips and discussion questions.

The Story of India - PBS.org: From ancient to modern times, India has played a central role in human history. The Story of India offers educational resources for teachers on this web site. The lessons are designed for high school world history

World History - OER Project: OER provides a collection of free activities, lesson plans, and other teaching resources related to topics in World History - such as Economic Networks and Trade, Cross Cultural Exchange, and Shifting Populations. These can be adapted for 6th graders or identified through a search of Middle School specific lessons.

Writings of the Ancient Maya - PBS Learning Media: In this interactive lesson supporting literacy skills, students are introduced to the ancient Mayan civilization through their writings. Students develop their literacy skills as they explore a social studies focus on the destruction of many Mayan writings by the Spanish and what archaeologists have learned from the writings that remain. During this process, they read informational text, learn and practice vocabulary words, and explore content through a video and interactive activities.
